title: LLM-based Multimodal Feedback Produces Equivalent Learning and Better Student Perceptions than Educator Feedback
venue: LAK 2026: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a real-time AI-facilitated multimodal feedback system can match or outperform educator-provided feedback in supporting learning. The authors focus on a longstanding educational problem: timely, specific, and actionable feedback is valuable for learning, but difficult for instructors to provide at scale, especially when feedback includes multiple modalities such as text, visuals, and audio. The study asks whether LLM-based multimodal feedback can support equivalent learning, how learners engage with it, and how they perceive its quality and value relative to business-as-usual educator feedback.

The intervention was a real-time AI feedback system embedded into an online learning workflow. It generated structured text feedback, retrieved the most relevant course slide page using retrieval-augmented generation, and offered optional AI audio narration. This treatment was compared against a baseline condition using fixed, prewritten educator feedback plus access to the same slide deck without targeted retrieval. Participants completed a pre-test, a learning-by-doing phase with immediate feedback, a post-test, and a post-survey. The experiment was conducted online through Qualtrics with random assignment to condition, and learner log data were collected to analyze engagement.

The population consisted of 197 U.S.-based college and university students recruited through Prolific, including students from diverse majors. The study context was an online, single-session crowdsourcing experiment centered on learning-science content about the multimedia principle in e-learning design. Participants were required to be at least 18 years old, currently enrolled in a college or university, and using a desktop or laptop computer. The paper does not clearly separate undergraduate from graduate participants, but the sample was drawn from higher education students.

The main conclusion is that AI multimodal feedback produced learning gains equivalent to educator feedback on objective pre/post assessments, while significantly improving student perceptions on several dimensions. Learners rated the AI feedback as clearer, more specific, more concise, more motivating, more satisfying, and lower in mental effort, with similar ratings for correctness, trust, and acceptance. Process logs suggested different engagement patterns by item type: educator feedback led to more retries on multiple-choice questions, while AI feedback appeared to support more revision on open-ended questions. The authors argue that such systems may reduce instructor workload while providing scalable, timely, and context-aware feedback, though they note the need for longer-term and more authentic classroom studies.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family models used to generate real-time multimodal educational feedback, including structured text feedback, retrieved slide references, and streamed audio narration.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies an AI-facilitated multimodal feedback system powered by OpenAI GPT-family models (gpt-5 for feedback generation and retrieval grounding; gpt-realtime API for streamed narration) to provide immediate corrective feedback during learning-by-doing activities, compared against educator-authored business-as-usual feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized online experiment, AI multimodal feedback produced significant pre/post learning gains within the treatment group (paired t=-5.6273, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.7623), but after controlling for pre-test scores, post-test performance did not differ significantly from educator feedback (ANCOVA F=0.91, p=0.34, partial η2=0.0047). This indicates equivalent learning outcomes relative to educator feedback rather than superiority.
findings.measure: Pre-test to post-test score change and ANCOVA-adjusted post-test scores on multimedia-principle learning tasks

findings.finding_summary: The AI system returned feedback very quickly, with median response time of 0.299 seconds for multiple-choice questions and 6.23 seconds for open-ended questions. Using a word-count proxy, the authors estimate the system is approximately 2.77× more time-efficient than authoring equivalent human text feedback (985/356 ≈ 2.77), though educator authoring time was not directly measured.
findings.measure: System response time and estimated authoring efficiency proxy
findings.effect_size: MCQ median=0.299s; OEQ median=6.23s; estimated efficiency≈2.77x

findings.finding_summary: Overall active-learning actions did not differ significantly between conditions (U=4075.5, p=0.0738), but engagement patterns varied by task type. For multiple-choice items, the educator-feedback group made more submit/update actions than the AI group (U=5660.5, p=0.02), whereas for open-ended items the AI group showed a trend toward more submissions (U=4060.5, p=0.066); total learning time also did not differ significantly (t=-0.413, p=0.680, Cohen's d=-0.062).
findings.measure: Submit/update action counts by question type and total learning time during learning-by-doing

findings.finding_summary: Compared with educator feedback, AI multimodal feedback led to lower reported mental effort (U=5190.50, p=0.0006) and higher satisfaction (U=3310.50, p=0.0240). Learners also rated AI feedback higher on specificity (U=2638.00, p=0.0001), clarity (U=3346.50, p=0.0199), simplicity (U=3246.00, p=0.0207), and motivation (U=3174.50, p=0.0146), while correctness (p=0.5378), trust (p=0.1456), and acceptance (p=0.2393) were comparable.
findings.measure: Post-survey Likert ratings of mental effort, satisfaction, perceived quality, motivation, trust, and acceptance

quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled online experiment with a reasonable sample (n=197) and clear comparative design, which supports stronger causal inference than correlational work. However, it was conducted in a short-term crowdsourcing setting rather than an authentic classroom, and some outcomes rely on self-report and proxy efficiency measures, so it falls short of blue-tier rigor.
impact_tier_rationale: The main academic result is equivalence rather than improvement over educator feedback (ANCOVA p=0.34, partial η2=0.0047), so learning impact is unclear despite positive within-group gains. Perception and efficiency outcomes are favorable, but the core learning effect relative to the comparator is not meaningfully positive.
